podcast.title: Emergence of Bands (Pre-1977)
podcast.body: Corporate rock describes a style of music exemplified by bands such as Boston and Kansas, which emerged as one of the various directions rock music had taken by 1977. "the so-called corporate rock bands like Boston and Kansas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Audience's Acceptance of Polish
podcast.body: Despite the critical "Corporate Rock" label, Foreigner's audience embraced the polished sound, considering it a defining and appealing characteristic of the band's music. "But to the band's audience, that polish was the whole point."

podcast.title: Critical Term for Foreigner's Sound
podcast.body: Critics frequently applied the term "Corporate Rock" to Foreigner, accusing the band of prioritizing slick production and large choruses over artistic risk, suggesting their music was commercially calculated. "Reviewers often called Forerner Corporate Rock, they accused the band of making it a priority to have slick production and big choruses over taking any sort of artistic risk."

podcast.title: Mainstream-Oriented Band Type
podcast.body: "Corporate rock band" was a term used to describe a project specifically put together with the explicit goal of being mainstream and maximizing record sales. Bands fitting this description, like Toto, were often considered "uncool" by certain segments of the rock audience, particularly the alt-rock crowd. "Toto was what we used to call a corporate rock band. The kind of project put together with the express purpose of being mainstream and selling as many records as possible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music Played by 1970s FM Radio
podcast.body: Corporate rock was the prevalent music played on most FM radio stations in the 1970s, featuring bands like Styx, Journey, and Boston. This style contrasted with the "alternative" programming that some stations began to introduce by occasionally playing punk or New Wave tracks. "So instead of just playing sticks and journey in Boston and what was called corporate rock, they added the occasional punk or new wave track."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
